items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose that we wish to approximate the area [MATH: \mathcal{A}] under the curve [MATH: y=x^2] on the interval [MATH: [1,4].]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f44327b2354d4b50353a64c5fd029b09]

Content:
We have already seen how to estimate the area using left and right Riemann sums, in which we approximate the area using rectangles.

Content:
However, we can get an even better estimate using trapezoids instead. The process of approximating the area under a curve using trapezoids is called the trapezoidal rule.

Content:
Here, we will cover the area under the graph of [MATH: y=x^2] with three trapezoids, each with a height equal to [MATH: 1,] as shown below. Note that the trapezoids are turned on their side, so their heights run horizontally.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c05175dfb98fe8f7aafebf84d74063af]

Content:
We compute the area of each trapezoid and add them all together:

Content:
[MATH: A|≈ [(f(1)+f(2)^(⏞)^(bases))/(2) ⋅ 1_(⏟)_(height)]^(⏞)^([math]1[/math]st trapezoid) + [(f(2)+f(3)^(⏞)^(bases))/(2) ⋅ 1_(⏟)_(height)]^(⏞)^([math]2[/math]nd trapezoid) + [(f(3)+f(4)^(⏞)^(bases))/(2) ⋅ 1_(⏟)_(height)]^(⏞)^([math]3[/math]rd trapezoid); = [(1^{2}+2^{2})/(2) ⋅ 1] + [(2^{2}+3^{2})/(2) ⋅ 1] + [(3^{2}+4^{2})/(2) ⋅ 1]; = 2.5 + 6.5 + 12.5; = 21.5]

Content:
Because the function is concave up over the interval [MATH: [1,4],] the trapezoids reach above the function, and therefore our approximation is an overestimate of the actual area.

Content:
In the previous problem, we had the following expression for the trapezoidal rule sum:

Content:
[MATH: \mathcal{A} \approx \dfrac{ {\color{red}f(1)}+{\color{red}f(2)} }{2}\cdot {\color{blue}\Delta x} + \dfrac{ {\color{red}f(2)}+ {\color{red}f(3)} }{2}\cdot {\color{blue}\Delta x} + \dfrac{ {\color{red}f(3)}+ {\color{red}f(4)} }{2}\cdot {\color{blue}\Delta x}]

Content:
Notice that we can simplify the above by factoring out [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}] and [MATH: \Delta x,] and also collecting like terms:
[MATH: \mathcal{A} \approx \dfrac{1}{2} [ \overbrace{{\color{red}f(1)} + 2\left( {\color{red}f(2)}+{\color{red}f(3)}\right) +{\color{red}f(4)}}^{\color{red}\large\text{bases}} ] \underbrace{\color{blue}\Delta x}_{\color{blue}\large\text{height}}]

Content:
In general, we can compute the trapezoidal rule sum for a function [MATH: y=f(x)] over an interval [MATH: [a,b]] using the general formula as follows:
[MATH: \mathcal{A} \approx \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot [\overbrace{{\color{red}f(a)} + 2({\color{red}f(x_1)}+{\color{red}f(x_2)}+ \ldots +{\color{red}f(x_{n-1})}) +{\color{red}f(b)} }^{\color{red}\large\text{bases}} ] \cdot\!\! \underbrace{\color{blue}\Delta x}_{\color{blue}\large\text{height}},]
Here, [MATH: n] is the number of trapezoids, and [MATH: \Delta x] is the step size given by
[MATH: \Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}.]

Content:
Note: If we look carefully at the formula, we realize that the trapezoidal rule is an average of the left and right Riemann sums!

[IMG: /graphics/dd04ee54b1306d80622dc7f51fc24f94]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: f(x)= 18 - x^2] and let [MATH: \mathcal A] denote the required area. The general formula for the trapezoidal rule states that [MATH: \mathcal{A} \approx \frac{1}{2}\left[f(a)+ 2\left(f(x_1) + f(x_2)+\ldots + f(x_{n-1})\right)+f(b) \right]\Delta x,] where [MATH: n] is the number of trapezoids and [MATH: \Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}] is the step size.

Here, we have the following values:

  • The number of trapezoids is [MATH: n=3.]

  • The corresponding interval is [MATH: [1,4],] so we have [MATH: a=1] and [MATH: b=4.]

  • The step size is given by [MATH: \Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n} = \dfrac{4 - 1}{3} = 1.]

Using the above values, the general formula becomes

[MATH: \mathcal{A} \approx \frac{1}{2}\left[f(1)+ 2\left(f(2) + f(3)\right) + f(4) \right]\cdot 1.]

To identify the function values, we now set up a table with the values of [MATH: x] and [MATH: f(x){:}]

[MATH: x]

[MATH: 1]

[MATH: 2]

[MATH: 3]

[MATH: 4]

[MATH: f(x)]

[MATH: 17]

[MATH: 14]

[MATH: 9]

[MATH: 2]

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

[MATH: \mathcal{A} \approx \frac{1}{2}\cdot\left[17 + 2\left(14 + 9\right)+ 2 \right]\cdot 1 = \dfrac{65}{2}]

Because the function is concave down over the interval [MATH: [1,4],] the trapezoids lie under the function, and therefore approximation is an underestimate of the correct area.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that we wish to approximate the area [MATH: \mathcal{A}] under the curve [MATH: y=x^2] on the interval [MATH: [1,4].]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f44327b2354d4b50353a64c5fd029b09]

Content:
We have already seen how to estimate the area using left and right Riemann sums, in which we approximate the area using rectangles.

Content:
However, we can get an even better estimate using trapezoids instead. The process of approximating the area under a curve using trapezoids is called the trapezoidal rule.

Content:
Here, we will cover the area under the graph of [MATH: y=x^2] with three trapezoids, each with a height equal to [MATH: 1,] as shown below. Note that the trapezoids are turned on their side, so their heights run horizontally.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c05175dfb98fe8f7aafebf84d74063af]

Content:
We compute the area of each trapezoid and add them all together:

Content:
[MATH: A|≈ [(f(1)+f(2)^(⏞)^(bases))/(2) ⋅ 1_(⏟)_(height)]^(⏞)^([math]1[/math]st trapezoid) + [(f(2)+f(3)^(⏞)^(bases))/(2) ⋅ 1_(⏟)_(height)]^(⏞)^([math]2[/math]nd trapezoid) + [(f(3)+f(4)^(⏞)^(bases))/(2) ⋅ 1_(⏟)_(height)]^(⏞)^([math]3[/math]rd trapezoid); = [(1^{2}+2^{2})/(2) ⋅ 1] + [(2^{2}+3^{2})/(2) ⋅ 1] + [(3^{2}+4^{2})/(2) ⋅ 1]; = 2.5 + 6.5 + 12.5; = 21.5]

Content:
Because the function is concave up over the interval [MATH: [1,4],] the trapezoids reach above the function, and therefore our approximation is an overestimate of the actual area.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The General Formula

Content:
In the previous problem, we had the following expression for the trapezoidal rule sum:

Content:
[MATH: \mathcal{A} \approx \dfrac{ {\color{red}f(1)}+{\color{red}f(2)} }{2}\cdot {\color{blue}\Delta x} + \dfrac{ {\color{red}f(2)}+ {\color{red}f(3)} }{2}\cdot {\color{blue}\Delta x} + \dfrac{ {\color{red}f(3)}+ {\color{red}f(4)} }{2}\cdot {\color{blue}\Delta x}]

Content:
Notice that we can simplify the above by factoring out [MATH: \dfrac{1}{2}] and [MATH: \Delta x,] and also collecting like terms:
[MATH: \mathcal{A} \approx \dfrac{1}{2} [ \overbrace{{\color{red}f(1)} + 2\left( {\color{red}f(2)}+{\color{red}f(3)}\right) +{\color{red}f(4)}}^{\color{red}\large\text{bases}} ] \underbrace{\color{blue}\Delta x}_{\color{blue}\large\text{height}}]

Content:
In general, we can compute the trapezoidal rule sum for a function [MATH: y=f(x)] over an interval [MATH: [a,b]] using the general formula as follows:
[MATH: \mathcal{A} \approx \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot [\overbrace{{\color{red}f(a)} + 2({\color{red}f(x_1)}+{\color{red}f(x_2)}+ \ldots +{\color{red}f(x_{n-1})}) +{\color{red}f(b)} }^{\color{red}\large\text{bases}} ] \cdot\!\! \underbrace{\color{blue}\Delta x}_{\color{blue}\large\text{height}},]
Here, [MATH: n] is the number of trapezoids, and [MATH: \Delta x] is the step size given by
[MATH: \Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}.]

Content:
Note: If we look carefully at the formula, we realize that the trapezoidal rule is an average of the left and right Riemann sums!

---

Item 3 — Example: Using the Trapezoidal Rule with Regular Step Size

Example Prompt:
Estimate the area under the curve [MATH: y=18-x^2] over the interval [MATH: [1,4]] using the trapezoidal rule with [MATH: 3] trapezoids of equal height.

[IMG: /graphics/dd04ee54b1306d80622dc7f51fc24f94]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: f(x)= 18 - x^2] and let [MATH: \mathcal A] denote the required area. The general formula for the trapezoidal rule states that
[MATH: \mathcal{A} \approx \frac{1}{2}\left[f(a)+ 2\left(f(x_1) + f(x_2)+\ldots + f(x_{n-1})\right)+f(b) \right]\Delta x,]
where [MATH: n] is the number of trapezoids and [MATH: \Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n}] is the step size.

Here, we have the following values:

- The number of trapezoids is [MATH: n=3.]
- The corresponding interval is [MATH: [1,4],] so we have [MATH: a=1] and [MATH: b=4.]
- The step size is given by
[MATH: \Delta x = \dfrac{b-a}{n} = \dfrac{4 - 1}{3} = 1.]

Using the above values, the general formula becomes

[MATH: \mathcal{A} \approx \frac{1}{2}\left[f(1)+ 2\left(f(2) + f(3)\right) + f(4) \right]\cdot 1.]

To identify the function values, we now set up a table with the values of [MATH: x] and [MATH: f(x){:}]

| [MATH: x] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 4] |
| [MATH: f(x)] | [MATH: 17] | [MATH: 14] | [MATH: 9] | [MATH: 2] |

Finally, we obtain the following approximation for our area:

[MATH: \mathcal{A} \approx \frac{1}{2}\cdot\left[17 + 2\left(14 + 9\right)+ 2 \right]\cdot 1 = \dfrac{65}{2}]

Because the function is concave down over the interval [MATH: [1,4],] the trapezoids lie under the function, and therefore approximation is an underestimate of the correct area.
